entries.name: Mexica (Aztec)
entries.settlement: causeway-linked island city on Lake Texcoco, ~200,000 people; a Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan
dwellings: adobe and stone palace compounds around patios
monuments: twin shrines of Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc
trade: tribute and pochteca caravan goods in (quetzal feathers, jade, cacao)
food, textiles and obsidian out
entries.beliefs: hundreds of gods led by Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc; the sun fed by blood; human sacrifice central to state ritual
entries.fell_by: Spanish conquest with Tlaxcalan allies, smallpox, siege of Tenochtitlan 1521
entries.notes: Names come from the tonalpohualli day-sign calendar. Pochteca merchant-spies ran long-distance trade and gathered intelligence.

entries.name: Maya
entries.region: Mesoamerica (Yucatan, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador)
entries.settlement: k'uhul ajaw city-states joined by sacbe (white limestone) causeways; plazas under temple-pyramids in tropical forest
dwellings: adobe and thatch pole-and-wattle houses around patios
stone elite palaces with corbel vaults
trade: cacao and salt everywhere
jade and obsidian in from highlands
cotton, feathers and pottery out
entries.beliefs: k'uhul ajaw (holy lords) mediating gods and ancestors; Itzamna, Chaak, K'inich Ajaw; bloodletting and the k'atun calendar
entries.fell_by: Classic collapse c. 800-900 (drought, war, overpopulation); Spanish conquest 1502-1697; never fully subdued in the lowlands
entries.notes: Only fully deciphered pre-Columbian script. ~30 Mayan languages are spoken today; the tzolk'in still runs alongside the haab calendar.

entries.name: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois Confederacy)
entries.settlement: longhouse villages under a matrilineal clan system; Grand Council of 50 hoyaneh (sachems) at Onondaga
trade: furs for European guns, cloth and tools
corn and tobacco within the League
wampum as diplomatic currency
entries.beliefs: Great Spirit; the Thanksgiving Address; Gaiwiio (Handsome Lake's reform faith, 1799)
entries.fell_by: not fallen; shattered by the American Revolution (1779 Sullivan expedition) and steady land loss
entries.notes: The Great Law of Peace (Gayanashagowa) bound five nations, later six, into a council democracy with clan mothers appointing chiefs.

entries.name: Ancestral Puebloans (Chaco, Mesa Verde)
entries.settlement: great houses and cliff dwellings; Chaco Canyon as a ceremonial-administrative centre linked by laser-straight roads
trade: turquoise and macaws from Mexico
jet, shell and copper bells in
pottery and maize circulated regionally
entries.beliefs: rain, ancestor and kiva-linked beliefs; great kivas aligned to solstices and lunar standstills
entries.fell_by: sustained drought (Great Drought 1276-1299), violence and out-migration; descendants are the modern Pueblo peoples
entries.notes: Chaco's great houses were aligned to lunar standstills. 'Anasazi' is a Navajo word for outsiders they dislike; use Ancestral Puebloans.

entries.name: Mississippian culture (Cahokia)
entries.region: Southeast and Midwest (Mississippi and Ohio valleys)
entries.settlement: temple-town mound centres; Cahokia peaked at 15,000-20,000, the largest city north of Mexico; Monks Mound rises ~30 m
trade: Mill Creek flint hoes across the Midwest
Great Lakes copper
Gulf marine shells
Appalachian quartz and mica
entries.beliefs: earth-fertility and solar cults; falcon/birdman imagery; communal feasts and mound mortuary ritual
entries.fell_by: population dispersal, environmental stress and violence c. 1300-1500; European diseases after 1500
entries.notes: Monks Mound is the largest pre-Columbian earthen structure in the Americas. The Southeastern Ceremonial Complex spread shared pan-regional styles.

entries.name: Inuit
entries.settlement: seasonal camps: semi-subterranean sod winter houses and caribou-hide summer tents (tupiq)
trade: skins and ivory for European goods (post-contact)
internal trade of seal oil, whale products and meteoric iron
entries.beliefs: animism: Sedna commands sea game; sila is weather and spirit; angakkuit (shamans) heal and recall game
entries.fell_by: not fallen; pressed by disease and 20th-century forced relocations and schooling
entries.notes: Descended from Thule migrants from Alaska c. 1000 CE who displaced the Dorset culture. 'Inuit' means 'the people'.

entries.name: Lakota (Oceti Sakowin)
entries.settlement: mobile tipi bands following bison; no towns; Sun Dance gatherings each summer
trade: bison robes and dried meat for guns, horses and metal goods
entries.beliefs: Wakan Tanka (the Great Mystery); White Buffalo Calf Woman brought the chanunpa pipe; vision quests
entries.fell_by: US conquest: treaty abrogation (Black Hills seizure 1877), Wounded Knee 1890, reservation system
entries.notes: Oceti Sakowin is the full confederation (Lakota, Dakota, Nakota). Horse culture and the bison made them the iconic Plains nation.

entries.name: Navajo (Dine)
subsistence: sheep and goat pastoralism (from 1600s Spanish stock)
entries.settlement: dispersed hogans (forked-pole, door east) across Dinetah; no towns; chapter houses today
trade: wool, blankets and jewellery for metal, cloth and horses
trading-post economy from the 1870s
entries.beliefs: hózhó (balance/beauty) restored by the Holy People's chantways; Changing Woman gave rise to the Dine
entries.fell_by: not fallen; Long Walk (1864-68, Bosque Redondo) and reservation poverty, but the nation endures
entries.notes: Dine means 'the people'. The largest federally recognised tribe in the US; Navajo Code Talkers were decisive in WWII.

entries.name: Cherokee
entries.settlement: square-ground towns of council houses; matrilineal clans; the 'seven mother towns'
dwellings: wattle-and-daub winter houses with bark roofs
crafts: Sequoyah's syllabary (1821) — mass literacy within years
trade: deerskins for European cloth and guns
orchards and salt sold to settlers
entries.beliefs: Unetlanvhi (Creator); balance across the three worlds; the di-ga-ni-gv-tli (medicine people)
entries.fell_by: not fallen; removal on the Trail of Tears (1838-39, ~4,000 dead); three federally recognised nations today
entries.notes: The syllabary made Cherokee among the fastest-literate nations on Earth; the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper launched 1828.

entries.name: Ojibwe (Anishinaabe)
entries.settlement: bands of wigwam villages around lakes and rice beds; semi-migratory with the seasons
trade: wild rice, furs and maple sugar for European goods
corn and tobacco middlemen
entries.beliefs: manitous in animals and places; the Midewiwin medicine society interprets dreams and power
entries.fell_by: not fallen; land cessions under US/Canada treaties (1837, 1854, 1863) and boarding-school assimilation
entries.notes: Anishinaabe means 'the original people'. The largest First Nation in Canada; the manoomin harvest still sets summer movements.

entries.name: Comanche
entries.region: Southern Great Plains (Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico)
entries.settlement: mobile horse-bands; no permanent towns; estate-style rendezvous camps
trade: the Comancheria supplied horses across the whole Southwest
bison robes
guns and metal for horses and hides
entries.beliefs: peyote rite (spread after 1800s contact) layered on older spirit beliefs
entries.fell_by: US military campaigns (Red River War 1874-75) and the destruction of the horse herds and bison
entries.notes: 'Lords of the Southern Plains': Comancheria was a de facto empire Spain, Mexico and the US treated as a peer power.

entries.name: Olmec
entries.settlement: ceremonial centres (San Lorenzo, La Venta, Tres Zapotes) on levees amid Gulf lowland swamps
trade: jade, obsidian and serpentine from far inland
cacao, rubber and pottery out
entries.beliefs: were-jaguar rain god; maize and rain fertility; rulers embodied as jaguars and feathered serpents
entries.fell_by: unknown; the centres were abandoned c. 400 BCE and absorbed into later Mesoamerican cultures
entries.notes: 'Mother culture' of Mesoamerica: writing, the calendar, the ballgame and state religion were largely born here.

entries.name: Teotihuacan
subsistence: chinampa and dry-farmed maize, beans, squash
entries.settlement: street-grid metropolis of ~125,000 along the Avenue of the Dead; corporate rule, apartment compounds, no deciphered kings
trade: obsidian fed all of Mesoamerica
jade, cacao, cotton and quetzal feathers in
manufactured goods exported as far as Tikal
entries.beliefs: Feathered Serpent and Great Goddess cults; Venus war symbolism; mass-sacrifice dedication rites
entries.fell_by: deliberate burning of the centre c. 550 CE — internal revolt or war; cause still debated
entries.notes: One of the largest cities on Earth in 500 CE. The later Aztecs found it in ruins and named it 'the place where the gods were created'.

entries.name: Zapotec
entries.settlement: hilltop capitals — Monte Alban, later Mitla and Zaachila; terrace-farmed city-states
dwellings: adobe and stone terrace houses around patios
crafts: the earliest writing in the Americas (~600 BCE)
trade: cochineal and cotton textiles out
obsidian, jade and quetzal feathers in
market hub between highlands and coast
entries.beliefs: Pitao Cozobi (maize), Pitao Cocijo (rain and lightning); Zapotec urn cult; ruler deification
entries.fell_by: Spanish conquest 1521-25 and epidemics; ~500,000 Zapotec speakers remain in Oaxaca today
entries.notes: Be'ena'a — 'the Cloud People'. Monte Alban's danzantes are the oldest monumental sculpture in Mesoamerica.

entries.name: Toltec
entries.settlement: militaristic capital at Tula ('Tollan'); colonnaded halls ruling through trade and war across Mesoamerica
trade: obsidian and turquoise for luxuries
jade and macaw feathers from the Gulf
Mayan jade-network routes reached
entries.beliefs: Quetzalcoatl as lawgiver-king (Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl); Venus war cult; heightened human sacrifice
entries.fell_by: Tula sacked c. 1150 (internal strife or Chichimec raids); the Aztecs claimed Toltec descent
entries.notes: 'Toltec' means 'master craftsman'. Legend said Topiltzin sailed east promising to return — the seed of the Cortes 1519 confusion. Topiltzin is semi-legendary.

entries.name: Adena culture
entries.region: Ohio Valley (Ohio, West Virginia, Indiana, Kentucky)
entries.settlement: small hamlets around conical burial mounds; no towns
monuments: conical burial mounds and circular earthworks
trade: Great Lakes copper and northern flint
Gulf shell
Appalachian mica
rare Rocky Mountain obsidian
entries.beliefs: ancestor and mortuary cult; bodies painted with red ochre; grave goods graded by rank
entries.fell_by: merged into the Hopewell tradition c. 100-200 BCE
entries.notes: Early mound builders already trading Rocky Mountain obsidian two millennia ago; ancestors of the Hopewell sphere.

entries.name: Hopewell tradition
entries.region: Ohio Valley and Midwest (Ohio, Illinois, Indiana)
entries.settlement: small dispersed villages plus giant geometric earthworks (Newark: octagon and great circle)
dwellings: bark-covered oval lodges in small villages
monuments: Newark Octagon and Great Circle earthworks
trade: obsidian from Wyoming and the Rockies
Great Lakes copper
Gulf shells
grizzly-bear teeth from the West
entries.beliefs: mortuary and peace-pipe smoking cult; art and earthworks tied to lunar and solar cycles
entries.fell_by: tradition dissolved c. 400-500 CE; successors unknown; replaced by Fort Ancient and Mississippian
entries.notes: The Newark Octagon is North America's most precisely aligned ancient observatory, keyed to the 18.6-year lunar standstill cycle.

entries.name: Hohokam
subsistence: irrigated maize, beans, squash and cotton
entries.settlement: canal-irrigated farm towns along the Salt and Gila rivers; platform-mound centres; hundreds of ballcourts
crafts: canal engineering (240 km of hand-dug channels)
trade: turquoise and shell west
macaws and copper bells from Mexico
Gulf of California shells
salt and cotton
entries.beliefs: ballcourts and plaza ritual shared with Mesoamerica; macaws point to Mexico-linked cults
entries.fell_by: canal system abandoned c. 1450 — silting, flood and drought; descendants are the O'odham (Pima, Tohono O'odham)
entries.notes: 'Those who have gone' in O'odham. One of the largest pre-industrial irrigation networks on Earth.

entries.name: Haida
entries.region: Haida Gwaii and southern Alaska panhandle
entries.settlement: large cedar longhouse villages in clan territories on exposed coasts; potlatch redistribution
crafts: formline art on poles, masks and bentwood boxes
trade: copper shields and eulachon oil via inland middlemen
dentalium shells
European metal post-1778 for potlatch wealth
entries.beliefs: Raven brought light and people; clan crests (Raven, Eagle); potlatch as law
entries.fell_by: not fallen; smallpox 1862 killed roughly half the Haida; potlatch outlawed 1885-1951
entries.notes: Haida Gwaii means 'Islands of the People'. The potlatch ban's repeal in 1951 sparked the formline revival.

entries.name: Tlingit
entries.settlement: clan longhouse villages at river mouths; moieties (Eagle/Raven) govern law and marriage
trade: eulachon (candlefish) oil from the Nass
Copper River copper
furs for European ships from 1785
entries.beliefs: Yeil (Raven) the trickster-creator; the dead return as orcas; clan-owned songs and crests
entries.fell_by: not fallen; the 1867 US purchase of Alaska brought canneries and mission suppression of clan law
entries.notes: 'The Tribe That Owns the Ice'. Koo.eex (potlatch) settled debts and raised heirs; US agents jailed potlatch hosts into the 1940s.

entries.name: Chinook (Columbia River)
entries.region: Lower Columbia River (Washington/Oregon) and its mouth
entries.settlement: towns of cedar plank houses on piling at trade choke-points; centre of the Columbia trade fair and the Jargon
trade: the emporium of the Northwest: dried salmon, canoes, berries and metal-bound European goods up and down the Columbia
entries.beliefs: First Salmon ceremony; Coyote the Transformer; cedar and salmon as kin
entries.fell_by: not fallen; malaria epidemics of the 1830s killed roughly 90%; promised treaties were never ratified
entries.notes: Chinook Jargon was the lingua franca of the whole Northwest; words like skookum and tillicum still appear in English there.

entries.name: Chumash
entries.settlement: large permanent villages (up to ~1,000 people) of sunken domed houses; tomol seafaring along the Channel
crafts: plank tomol canoes stitched like sewn boats
trade: seaborne trade along the coast and islands
soapstone and steatite to inland peoples for shell beads and obsidian
salt and fish oil
entries.beliefs: Hutash the earth mother; tomol spirit guidance; cave paintings as shamanic star calendars
entries.fell_by: not fallen; Spanish missions (1769-1834) and disease; most Chumash groups still seek federal recognition
entries.notes: The tomol crossed 30 km of the Santa Barbara Channel for eight millennia; the 'Phoenicians of California'.

entries.name: Powhatan (Tsenacommacah)
entries.settlement: Werowocomoco, capital of ~30 tributary towns over Tsenacommacah; werowances (commanders) under a paramount chief
trade: food and furs for English beads, copper and hatchets
internal tribute of corn, skins and shells to Werowocomoco
entries.beliefs: Okee (storm and death); Ahone (benevolent creator, unworshipped); animist priests (quiocos)
entries.fell_by: English colonisation; wars 1610-46; land loss in Virginia; surviving tribes federally recognised 2018
entries.notes: Wahunsenacawh ruled ~30 tribes and 14,000-21,000 people at Jamestown's 1607 landing; 'Pocahontas' is Matoaka, fame ~12-14 in 1607.

entries.name: Hopi
entries.settlement: stone pueblo villages on three mesa tops (Walpi, Oraibi, Shungopavi); matrilineal clans; Oraibi inhabited continuously since c. 1100
monuments: Oraibi (Walpi parish villages on the Hopi mesas)
trade: blue corn and piki bread for Navajo wool blankets
salt and pottery for buckskin
entries.beliefs: katsinim mediate rain and ancestors; Spider Woman taught weaving; the Emergence from the Sipapu
entries.fell_by: not fallen; Spanish mission suppression (1629-91) and US pressure, but the Hopi mesas were never stormed
entries.notes: Oraibi is possibly the oldest continuously inhabited settlement in the United States.

entries.name: Blackfoot (Siksika)
entries.region: Northern Plains (Montana, Alberta; Siksika, Kainai, Piikani)
entries.settlement: migratory band camps on the plains; winter in sheltered coulees; summer Sun Dance gatherings
trade: pemmican and bison robes for guns and metal
horse trade drives expansion
entries.beliefs: Naapi (Old Man) the culture hero; Thunder and Sun powers
entries.fell_by: not fallen; whisky-trade devastation, bison extermination (1880s) and the 1877/1888 treaties
entries.notes: Siksika likely means 'black-footed', after their moccasins. Fort Whoop-Up nearby opened the Cypress Hills massacre of 1873.

entries.name: Seminole
entries.settlement: scattered chickee (open-sided stilt palm-thatch house) camps hidden in swamp and Everglades
trade: deerskins and furs for European guns, metal tools and cloth
entries.beliefs: Creek-derived Green Corn ceremony (Busk); medicine and herbal knowledge
entries.fell_by: not fallen; wars 1816-18, 1835-42, 1855-58; ~3,000 removed on the Trail of Tears; the 'Unconquered' survived in the Everglades
entries.notes: Formed from Creek (Mikasuki) groups plus Black maroons. The Seminole never signed a peace treaty with the US.

entries.name: Taíno
entries.region: Greater Antilles (Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Cuba, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.settlement: cacicazgos (chiefdoms) around plazas and conuco farms; villages up to ~1,000; Yucayeques
trade: cassava and island crafts
tribute food to caciques
after 1492: forced gold and pearl labour
entries.beliefs: zemis (ancestor and deity stones); Yocahu (cassava lord) and Atabey; cohoba trance rituals
entries.fell_by: Spanish colonisation, slavery and smallpox 1492-1550; absorbed into island society
entries.notes: They gave the world hammock, barbecue (barbacoa), canoe, hurricane (juracan) and tobacco. Genetic studies find strong Taíno maternal DNA in Puerto Ricans.

entries.name: Kalinago (Island Caribs)
entries.region: Lesser Antilles (Dominica, St Vincent, Grenada, Trinidad)
entries.settlement: hilltop and river-mouth defensive villages behind palisades; councils led by ouboutou (war captains)
trade: raid-and-trade economy dominating the narrow islands 1492-1650
manioc beer and cotton for European metal
entries.beliefs: ancestral tobacco-smoking rites and spirit-world (matoutou) cults; the sea mother is invoked by seafarers
entries.fell_by: not fallen; extermination wars and disease; Dominica's Kalinago Territory (est. 1903) survives
entries.notes: 'Caribs' to Europeans — the root of 'Caribbean'. They held the Lesser Antilles against Spain for a century and kept them native-held into the 1600s. Names were rarely recorded; early Spanish and French records are the only witness.

entries.name: Mi'kmaq
entries.region: Atlantic Canada (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, PEI, Gaspe, Newfoundland)
entries.settlement: seasonal coastal camps; family hunting territories in seven 'districts' governed by the Mi'kmaq Grand Council
trade: furs and fish oil for France and Britain from the 1600s
salmon guiding and basketmaking later
entries.beliefs: Glooscap the culture hero; sky-world creation; Catholic syncretism
entries.fell_by: not fallen; land cessions, disease and residential schools — the Peace and Friendship Treaties never ceded land
entries.notes: 'The People' / 'Allied Peoples'. First allies of New France; their hunting and fishing rights remain constitutionally protected in Canada.

entries.name: Norse (Vinland)
entries.settlement: one confirmed base camp: eight turf buildings with iron furnaces and boat repair; brief occupation c. 990-1050
trade: walrus ivory and furs back to Greenland
barter with Indigenous 'Skrælings'
entries.beliefs: Norse paganism; Thor, Odin, Freyr
entries.fell_by: Skræling hostility, Greenland isolation, abandonment by ~1050
entries.notes: The sagas told of grapes and wild wheat; only the Newfoundland base is archaeologically confirmed — Markland and Helluland remain debated sites.

entries.name: Metis
entries.region: Canadian Prairies (Red River, Manitoba; western Canada, northern US)
entries.settlement: river-lot farms along the Red and Assiniboine; mobile buffalo-hunt camps
trade: pemmican for the fur trade
buffalo robes and furs
carts hired to trading companies
entries.beliefs: Catholicism woven with Cree and Ojibwe spirit tradition; fiddle-dance and jig
entries.fell_by: not fallen; defeated at Batoche 1885, Riel hanged, scrip land-claim frauds scattered the nation
entries.notes: The first new nation of the fur trade. The Red River cart — wood axles, no iron — swam rivers and outlasted horseback freight.

entries.name: Gullah (Geechee)
entries.region: Sea Islands and coast (South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, North Carolina)
entries.settlement: rice-plantation task-system villages on the Sea Islands, preserving West African culture
trade: rice and Sea Island cotton for Atlantic markets
Senegambian rice knowledge built the Carolina economy
entries.beliefs: Yoruba and Kongo ancestor reverence fused with Baptist Christianity; root doctors and hoodoo
entries.fell_by: not fallen; survived slavery, Jim Crow and beach development; ~125,000 speakers on the coast
entries.notes: Gullah/Geechee are English-based creoles keeping African grammar. 'Geechee' is the inland-Georgia name. Carolina Gold rice techniques travelled with Senegambian captives.

entries.name: Cajun (Acadiana)
entries.settlement: long narrow riverfront farm strips (French rang system) along the bayous
trade: rice, sugar and indigo historically
fish, crawfish and duck towards New Orleans
muskrat pelts
entries.beliefs: Roman Catholic, syncretic with folk healing (traiteurs — faith healers)
entries.fell_by: not fallen; expelled from Acadia in the Grand Derangement (1755), re-settled in Spanish Louisiana from 1765
entries.notes: Cajun French survives only in Louisiana; French schools were outlawed into the 1920s until the immersion revival.

entries.name: Californio
entries.region: Alta California (San Diego to San Francisco)
entries.settlement: small pueblos (San José, Los Angeles, Monterey) and vast ranchos with adobe haciendas
trade: hides and tallow to Boston 'hide ships'
wine, olive oil and citrus to Mexico
sea otter pelts to Russia and China
entries.beliefs: Roman Catholic (mission system, neophyte Indigenous labour)
entries.fell_by: not fallen; US conquest 1846-48 and the Gold Rush buried the rancho world
entries.notes: 'Buckaroo' is vaquero anglicised. Hide-and-tallow California supplied New England's shoe industry; Vallejo's Sonoma hacienda was the elegant capital of the rancho world.

entries.name: Pennsylvania Dutch
entries.settlement: small family farms with bank barns and stone farmhouses; Amish enclaves keep horse-and-buggy discipline
trade: wheat and flour to Philadelphia for export
hemp and iron
dairy
entries.beliefs: German Reformed and Lutheran mainstream; Anabaptist Amish, Mennonite and Brethren horse-and-buggy communities
entries.fell_by: not fallen; absorbing into mainstream America; the Amish have doubled to ~400,000 in the last 50 years
entries.notes: 'Dutch' is a corruption of Deutsch — they are Germans. Conrad Weiser was the indispensable go-between of Haudenosaunee and Pennsylvania diplomacy.

entries.name: Klondike stampeders
subsistence: packed beans, bacon and flour (a ton per man)
entries.settlement: boom camps over the Chilkoot and White Passes; Dawson City swelled to ~30,000 in 1898
crafts: placer gold mining (rocker, long tom, sluice)
trade: everything hauled over the pass: beans, bacon, whiskey, picks
steamboats via St. Michael, Alaska
entries.beliefs: no single faith — American Protestant and secular fortune-seeking mix; First Nations charged tolls and guided the trail
entries.fell_by: the gold played out; stampeders dispersed to Nome (1899) and beyond
entries.notes: ~100,000 set out, ~30,000 arrived, ~4,000 found gold. Jack London mined one season before going home to write.
